title: Jury at inquest into death of man who died at Barton jail makes 18 recommendations
subtitle: Thirty-year-old died in 2017 at Hamilton-Wentworth Detention Centre
article: The jury at the inquest into the death of Ryan McKechnie has made 18 recommendations to prevent overdose deaths at the Hamilton-Wentworth Detention Centre and better support families after a death.

The 34-year-old died on June 29, 2017, after about seven months at the Barton Street jail. His sister Amy McKechnie learned about his death after news spread over social media while she was in hospital because their father died the same day. She has been pushing for answers and accountability ever since.

Ryan's death was originally supposed to be part of a super inquest last fall that examined six deaths at the jail, but that inquest was held virtually, something Amy found impersonal. After pushing for an in-person inquest, one was held at the Coroners Courts in Toronto the last week of January.
The inquest was emotional and revealing, Amy said, calling it a "pretty heavy" experience.
The jury found Ryan died of an accidental overdose of a combination of drugs, including fentanyl.

A day before his overdose death, guards did a sweep of his cell and one of his cellmates was found with contraband. There was also an unidentified substance open in the cell, the inquest heard. That inmate was placed in a dry cell - one with no running water so inmates can't conceal or flush contraband hidden in body cavities.

Ryan and another inmate went through the body scanner twice, but were allowed to remain together in their cell. While the other inmate's scan showed anomalies, it was inconclusive. The next morning, Ryan never woke for breakfast, and soon after his cellmate was banging on the doors to catch the correctional officer's attention. But it was too late, and Ryan was pronounced dead.
Had Ryan been separated and placed in a dry cell too, Amy believes he would not have died.

The recommendations include: better training and practices around body scanners; trauma-informed supports and improved communication with families following a death; more thorough checks to ensure inmates are not in distress when correctional officers do rounds; and separating and more closely monitoring all inmates who shared a cell where contraband was detected.

The inquest was mandatory under the Coroners Act, because he died in custody. Inquest recommendations are not binding, but agencies must post publicly what steps they are taking (or not) to follow recommendations.
The super inquest last fall led to 56 recommendations to improve access to health care, programming and harm reduction, all meant to help prevent similar deaths.

That inquest heard issues at the jail had persisted despite a similar inquest in 2018 into eight overdose deaths. Despite six years passing between the super inquests, the 2024 inquest heard 27 of those earlier recommendations had still not been fully implemented and some jail staff said they were not even aware of the earlier inquest.

Amy said the inquest into her brother's death was emotional and did provide answers. However, inquests are not about determining fault, a process she found frustrating because she believes evidence uncovered shows some negligence.
Following the inquest, she says she is now looking into the possibility of a class-action lawsuit.
